subtopic: STATEMENT ON DISCUSSIONS WITH U.S. PRESIDENT

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: STATEMENT ON DISCUSSIONS WITH U.S. PRESIDENT
speechtext:
Following the usual custom I intend to make a statement concerning some of the matters which were discussed between President Kennedy and myself, in order to amplify to some extent the terms of the communique which, as is the case with all communiques-and I emphasize the comprehensiveness of that statement-did not cover in particular, or deal in detail, with what has taken place, for reasons which will be obvious to most people.
The President placed before parliament his views on certain major issues before us, and what he said to me personally was, of course, consistent with what he said in parliament although amplified in considerable detail. The scope of the discussions was set forth in the communique. While the nature of some of the subjects discussed denies that they be given public utterance, I think I can properly report on some of the main topics of the discussion.
As far as the world situation in general is concerned, there is a continuing crisis as the Soviet union wages its campaign for global domination, and the dust clouds of soft words and the periodic soft answers must not be allowed to delude anyone into believing that the Soviet challenge will not continue with unabated, or even increased, determination. However, today an announcement was made which all the world hopes will lead to an amelioration of relations between east and west. I refer, of course, to the prospective meeting between the President of the United States and Chairman Krushchev. Immdiately on his arrival, when we met together personally, the President gave me that information, and we both expressed the hope that out of that meeting in Vienna in consequence of the personal exchange of views might come, in the interests of humanity as a whole, that degree of agreement which has been the expectation and the hope of manking since 1946.
As far as our relations with the United States and the western hemisphere are concerned, President Kennedy laid strong emphasis on them, both in his public and in his
private discussions. We reviewed the problems facing all the countries of North and South America, and noted the situation, among a number of these countries, in connection with different ranges and stages of economic development, and the special situations in regard to their social and political structures which have such a bearing on both their development and stability.
The President would welcome Canada's participation in the organization of American states. This, of course, has been discussed and was recently discussed in this house by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. So far as this question is concerned, which has been a continuing one throughout the year for the consideration of governments of Canada, it is still in that category and, of course, no commitments were made, or would be made, without parliament being made aware in advance of any such action.
I was much impressed with the emphasis which the President placed on the importance of the problems confronting our two countries' hemispheric affairs. I assured him that his views would be the subject of serious consideration. I referred to his reviews respecting membership in the organization of American states and the other problems that are incidental to that membership, and I should hope, that at an early date parliament will have the opportunity, if it so desires, of discussing this question.
With reference to Cuba, I made it clear to the President that the Canadian government has no intention of acting as mediator between the United States and Cuba. Indeed, as stated before, there was no foundation for the press report that such an offer had been put forward.
We discussed the affairs of southeast Asia, and particularly the situation in Laos and South Viet Nam. We are agreed on the objective of establishing a truly independent and neutral Laos, and of the necessity of securing general support for effective control machinery; because only if this is done will the Laos situation be resolved and peace and stability attained in southeast Asia. We discussed the experience of the international control and supervisory commissions, on which Canada has been serving, and the vital importance of the role of these commissions was emphasized.
It is natural that the question of Chinese representation in the United Nations at the next session of the general assembly should

External Affairs
have been canvassed, and we agreed to consult together, therefore, in the next few months in respect of this subject, because it will not come up for consideration until September.
The policies and programs of our countries in relation to underdeveloped nations received attention. We recognize that we now have, in the development assistance group, a new forum for reviewing and co-ordinating our programs in this field. I placed before the President, with some degree of pride, the outstanding record of Canada in aiding other countries since the end of world war II, and I also pointed out the very substantial increase in Colombo aid and in the general scale of aid that has been given since 1958.
There was some considerable discussion in the field of economic affairs. I pointed out that Canada has a tremendous balance of payments deficit in commodity trade, and that this was a matter that had to be resolved. Each of our countries is by a wide margin the other's most important trading partner. With the great volume and complexity of our economic relations it is realized that problems will arise, but what is of paramount importance is that these problems be met through discussion, by regular consultation and free exchanges of views and the continuing spirit of good will.
The European economic community and the tariff relationships now being worked out were discussed at length. Both countries have been working actively to ensure that trading relationships with this community should favour the maintenance and development of a large volume of trade in each direction. The importance of trading relationships with Europe would be considerably enhanced if the United Kingdom government decided to join the Six in the common market.
The problem that is common to both of us, namely farm surpluses, especially wheat, was discussed. We agreed to continue to work closely together in this field. I know the house will endorse the views expressed by the President on Wednesday about food surpluses and how to make constructive use of them. The food for peace program already embodies many of those ideas. I express my appreciation of the support which the United States has given to the Canadian suggestion for a food bank made at the U.N. and the F.A.O. My expectation is that some more specific proposals in this regard will be placed before the United Nations assembly in September.
Questions of defence were discussed mostly in connection with NATO. Emphasis was laid
tMr. Diefenbaker.]
on the increase in the capability of the alliance to wage war defensively with conventional forces in order to reduce the likelihood of having to rely more extensively upon nuclear weapons for defence.
In so far as NATO is concerned, the views I expressed to the President were that with a population of about 400 million people and with a gross national product four tims that of the Soviet union, the NATO nations possess great strength, but that the strengthening of unity in NATO is a continuing imperative and must not be neglected. I believe that the leaders of the NATO countries will have to advance further than the steps already taken to strengthen wider unity, not only in defence but economically and even politically.
The position of affairs in West Berlin was discussed. It is of great importance to Canada, and Canadians should realize this fact; for Canada has undertaken, along with its NATO allies, serious commitments in regard to West Berlin and the maintenance of the freedom of the people of that city.
The President told me of what was taking place in Geneva from the point of view of the United States, and of the endeavour in particular to reach agreement on a pact to end nuclear testing. I believe that as we endeavour to bring about disarmament, an effective treaty to end nuclear testing is a basic step before any disarmament of a more general character can be achieved. I believe we must continue to press for controlled disarmament and in particular, in the light of the progress of the last few years in the upper skies and the recent achievements of Commander Shepard and Major Gagarin, we face the stern fact that without international control of space the future will be even more perilous than the present.
In so far as our purposes are concerned, I am of those who have advocated not only to the President but on other occasions that we in the free world should explain our purposes, our ideals, our aims, to the non-committed world to a degree that we have not done heretofore. I found in my trip to Asia some years ago that too often the interpretation of what we stand for has been left to the whims of the communists. Indeed, I believe that in 1918 when President Wilson made his declaration, and again in 1941 with the Atlantic charter, these declarations had a tremendous effect; and I feel that today the ideals of the free world should be restated in simple terms so that all mankind will know that we have joined in a declaration of principles, and that all with recognize in these principles the equality of races and will condemn discrimination in any form.
I think all of us were very pleased at the manner in which Canadians received the

President and his wife. I want to say particularly now much I appreciated the fact that, while no arrangements had been made for him to meet the members of this house and the other place, as soon as I suggested it to him on the evening of his arrival he said he fully understood that this would be the proper course to follow and in keeping with the responsibility discharged by the parliamentarians of this country. We recognize President Kennedy as the courageous, inspiring leader of the free world. He bears a tremendous burden. His concern is great: his dedication is great. I think our meeting together was worth while in every sense of the word, for it underlined that spirit of co-operation between our nations that is a model for all mankind.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON DISCUSSIONS WITH U.S. PRESIDENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am sure all members of the house are grateful to the Prime Minister for the statement he has made, and which gives some indication of the extensive character of the discussions between himself and the President of the United States on the occasion of the latter's visit to our country. As the Leader of the Opposition said, speaking outside this house, the visit of the President of the United States was both a happy and an important event. It was to be hoped that the agreeable character of this visit was shared not only by Canadians but by citizens of the United States generally. It is well that we should underline the importance of a visit from the head of state and the head of government of the most powerful country in the free world. This visit of President Kennedy will take its place with the visits of some of his predecessors, notably President Roosevelt, President Truman and President Eisenhower.
The Prime Minister has said that the communique which followed the discussions between the two heads of government was of such a general character that it should not be presumed to have covered even in any measure of generality the discussions which took place between him and the President. I am sure the Prime Minister will not misunderstand me if I say that while his statement this morning was much more extended than was the communique itself, nevertheless the statement this morning likewise is in such general terms that it is not possible to derive a clear appreciation of the full nature of the discussions that took place. I am not complaining; the character of international affairs requires that negotiations should at certain stages be conducted in secret. However, it is only proper to point out that the range of subjects which formed the basis of discussion between the President
External Affairs
and the Prime Minister was of such a character as to give us at this time not much more than an indication of the nature of the discussions.
It is important to note that the Prime Minister said the June confrontation between President Kennedy and Chairman Khrushchev was a matter that was mentioned during their talks. This is an extremely important development. We can only hope that the necessary preparations will attend both President Kennedy and Chairman Khrushchev in this very important meeting which, I take it, is not of the nature of a summit meeting in the sense in which that meeting was understood last May. It is to be a brief meeting between the two heads of government. In any event, I am sure the Prime Minister would want Canadians generally to note that too much should not be expected from such a meeting. It would be better to have concrete results flow unexpectedly rather than to raise the anticipations of the Canadian and other nations and their peoples.
The Prime Minister said that he and the President discussed matters having to do with our relations with South and Central America. Indeed, in his memorable statement in this house the President called upon Canada to share to an even greater measure the responsibilities of hemispheric consultation and direction. The statement he made about Canadian participation in the organization of American states was couched in such terms as to warrant one in believing he had some reason for thinking that the government was going to make an important decision in this regard.
As the Prime Minister has said, it is not without significance that in the foreign affairs debate in this house two weeks ago, proposals were made for Canadian participation in the organization of American states, notably by the Leader of the Opposition. Since that time there has been a manifestation of increasing Canadian interest in the participation by Canada in the organization of American states and at the same time, in the face of what the Prime Minister has said today and what the President of the United States said in his speech here on Wednesday last, it would seem that the Canadian government is giving active consideration to participation in the organization of American states. If the government does announce its intention to participate in the organization of American states, the Prime Minister may be assured, it will receive the support of the members of the party on whose behalf I am now speaking, for we believe that the time has come when this step should be taken.
The Prime Minister referred to a whole series of other matters that were discussed,

External Affairs
including the situation in Asia and the situation in the Caribbean, as well as that in South America and in Central America and the admission of communist China to the United Nations. In that regard it is significant that the Prime Minister this morning said that further discussions between Canada and the United States will take place regarding this matter. The Prime Minister did not say whether, in his discussions with the President, note had been taken of the recent arrangements made with communist China for the sale of Canadian wheat and the relation of that arrangement, as noted by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, to the matter of Canadian recognition or Canadian acceptance of communist China in the United Nations.
Without traversing all the matters that were mentioned, among them the relation of the United States and Canada to the common market, I can only say that undoubtedly the Prime Minister meant to emphasize this morning the fact that he fully agreed with the President in what the latter had said as to the importance the government of the United States attaches to the organization known as O.E.C.D., which provides a liaison between certain countries, notably the United States and Canada, and the common market.
This visit of the President of the United States has come at a very important time in the administration of the new President. It has come at a very important time in the history of the world. This statement of the Prime Minister, couched in general terms, gives Canadians an opportunity of once again expressing their gratitude to the President for his visit and of once again affirming the friendship which this country has for the United States, recognizing as we do that an understanding between our two countries is essential in our own interests as well as in the interests of other countries which desire to see peace maintained at this time.
I should like to say that the words of the Prime Minister in this regard are echoed not only by those who sit on the treasury benches but by those of us who sit in the opposition and, I am sure, by the Canadian people generally. We are happy over this visit of the young President of the United States. We are happy because he affirmed the friendship of his country for us, and because he gave us an opportunity of letting him know that in matters of great moment at this critical time in human affairs, Canada understands not only its own responsibilities but those of the United States and other free countries which are anxious to pursue policies designed to maintain peace among the nations in this turbulent period of world affairs.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON DISCUSSIONS WITH U.S. PRESIDENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the visit to Canada of President Kennedy and his charming wife has been welcomed by all Canadians. The warmth of the reception given to the President and Mrs. Kennedy indicates the very friendly relationship between our country and the United States.
President Kennedy, when he spoke in this chamber, did so in a very forthright manner and left no room for misunderstanding about the attitude of the United States to important international events. I had expected the President of the United States to give us when he spoke here, as he did, in clear and concise terms the position of the United States on many vexing world problems. But I am not at all certain that when the President made it so clear to us what he wished Canada to do with regard to certain important and controversial problems, it was of assistance to Canadians in coming to a conclusion. I say this because the conclusions that we come to on these important questions must, most clearly, be our decisions made on the basis of what we believe to be in the interests of freedom, the improvement of living standards of the people of the world, and of peace.
The President made it clear that from his point of view he wished to see NATO strengthened, not only in the role of conventional weapons but also as far as nuclear armaments are concerned, and that he was prepared to sit down and consider the working out of some arrangement, I take it to broaden the control of nuclear weapons in the hands of NATO forces and forces attached to NATO.
While there may be some difference of opinion among the C.C.F. people and others who are interested in the New party on the question of NATO, there has been no difference at all in our attitude toward handing to NATO and all its members nuclear weapons to be placed in the hands of NATO troops. We oppose this particular policy, and should this be the policy adopted by the NATO organization we shall certainly oppose it when it is undertaken. NATO continues to be strictly a military organization, and over the years we have emphasized that article II was the part of the NATO treaty that we wished to see expanded and developed.
The President made reference to O.E.C.D., as did the Prime Minister this morning. We think this organization is important. We think Canada should play a most active part, and we hope that O.E.C.D. will see the economic development of the north Atlantic area, and from O.E.C.D. can go some of the economic help that will improve living standards in large areas of the world.

The President had another important proposition to put before us. That was his view with regard to the organization of American states. The Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs have said that the government is giving careful consideration to whether or not Canada should decide to join the organization of American states.
I said in this house on a previous occasion that in my view the time had come for Canada to join the organization of American states. However, I am prepared, with the Prime Minister, to give further consideration to this most important question; because while I do see some advantage in being a member of the organization of American states in a time when we are able to deal in a cool and collected manner with the economic problems of the hemisphere, it does seem to me there may be a temptation on the part of some to develop the organization of American states to maintain the status quo in certain South American countries. Or even worse still, some may hope that it can be developed into a military organization, which we think would be a very serious mistake. We are considering this question as is the government, and we think the government is correct in giving the Canadian nation ample time to consider the pros and cons before making any decision to join this- organization.
There was one important statement made by the Prime Minister this morning which I was sorry to hear. It was that there was no truth in the newspaper reports that our Secretary of State for External Affairs had offered to mediate between Cuba and the United States. I think such an offer from Canada would have been wise. We can now see that the United States would have quickly rejected it. None the less it does seem to me that in the interests of peace and in the interests of the economic development of the hemisphere there must be some mediation in the conflict between Cuba and the United States. If we are to keep communism out of the western hemisphere, as we all wish to do, we must not be found on the side of dictators, on the side of vested interests and opposed to the improvement of health, education and living standards of the people of Latin America.
The Prime Minister went on to make some reference to China. He referred to the need to reconsider the admission of China to the United Nations. The Canadian government has said there can be no recognition of China. I think that Canada is, in an economic sense, recognizing China. It would seem to me that
Controls on Japanese Trade to undertake trade relations of a very extensive kind with China is in fact a type of recognition.
No less a person than Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent was reported in the press as having said that in light of the trade relations being developed between Canada and China he thought it only sensible that representatives of our country should be stationed in China and representatives of China should be stationed in Canada. We think this is a sensible attitude, and that it is only a matter of time before we do grant this type of formal diplomatic recognition to China, from which we think would flow improved and increased trade with China.
The President went on to emphasize-and in this we wholeheartedly agree-the need for those nations in the western world which have high standards of living to give a part of their production to improve the economic standards of people in less fortunate countries. The Prime Minister says that Canada has a good record in this regard. I will not dispute that but I will say that Canada's record should be much better than it is; that a record of $70 million or $75 million of economic assistance during the current fiscal year is not enough; that the figure of 1 per cent of the gross national product mentioned by the President of the United States is something for which we could well strive. I am convinced that by providing economic assistance we could do more than in any other field toward maintaining peace and improving economic relations amongst the peoples of the world.
We are glad, Mr. Speaker, that the President of the United States and Mrs. Kennedy have made this visit to Ottawa.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON VOLUNTARY CONTROLS ON EXPORTS TO CANADA

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT ON VOLUNTARY CONTROLS ON EXPORTS TO CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to table copies of a letter, dated May 15, which I have received from the ambassador of Japan informing me of the voluntary restraints the Japanese government has decided to apply on the export of certain products to Canada for the year 1961. These decisions have been taken by the Japanese government following extensive consultations with the government of Canada. I assume the house will wish to have this letter printed as an appendix to Hansard. The comparable information concerning the Japanese voluntary controls for 1960 is found as an appendix to Hansard of May 5, 1960.
Perhaps I might make a few comments on the arrangements which have been made for

Controls on Japanese Trade 1961. It will be recalled that in 1959 and 1960 the Japanese government extended its voluntary controls to cover a wider range of textile products. Controls were maintained in 1960 on cotton fabrics, most cotton made-up goods, various garments of spun rayon and other synthetic fabrics and bedspreads and elastics of all fibres. All these products will, of course, remain under control this year. It has also been decided to add several new items to the list of products under quota control, namely dish towels, ladies' fabric dress gloves, nylon fabric and certain types of ribbons. Several quota categories which covered groups of miscellaneous products have been divided into smaller categories in order to avoid the risk of undue concentration on particular products. For several particularly sensitive textile products the quotas for 1961 are somewhat lower than for 1960, while for certain other products provision has been made for a moderate increase. The details of the arrangements for textiles are to be found in annex A to the ambassador's letter.
In mid-1960 Japan introduced for the first time a system of voluntary restraints on rubber footwear and rubber-soled canvas footwear. The levels of shipment in 1960 were not established on the basis of consultation between the two governments. For 1961, however, the Japanese government has consulted us about the nature and levels of the quotas to be applied on these products. The details will be found in annex B to the ambassador's letter.
There will now be two categories, waterproof footwear and canvas footwear. The category known as canvas footwear will now include shoes with rubber soles and fabric uppers of any kind. In particular it will include rubber-soled shoes with corduroy or velveteen uppers, which have been shipped to Canada in considerable quantity over the past six months. In order to make allowance for some of the shipments of these shoes which took place before the revised definition was adopted, a special quota of 360,000 pairs has been established for this year only. This is in addition to the basic quota on this product of 2,200,000 pairs.
As the house is aware, exports of plywood from Japan to Canada have been subject to voluntary export control for several years. Owing to the difficulty of predicting market demand for this product for the full year, the quota outlined in annex C relates only to the first six months of 1961. Further consultations will take place in relation to the quota for the second half of this year.
Although stainless steel flatware was first placed under voluntary export control in 1959, the Canadian flatware industry has

continued to experience difficulty as a result of the volume of imports. Accordingly the Japanese government has taken the exceptional step of reducing significantly the export quota for 1961 below that for 1960. The figures appear in annex D.
In addition to rubber footwear several other items are placed under quota to Canada this year for the first time. These are transistor radios, radio and television receiving tubes, vinyl raincoats and polyester staple buttons. The arrangements for these products are set out in annexes E to H to the ambassador's letter.
The various measures described in this letter are being undertaken by the government of Japan in conformity with its established policy or promoting the orderly growth of Japanese exports to the Canadian market. May I say that I share the belief expressed by the ambassador that this policy of self restraint should pave the way for further expansion of two way trade on an orderly basis, to the mutual benefit of both countries.

speechtext: The statement which has been made by the Minister of Finance is an important one, since it has to do with quotas in connection with trade between Canada and Japan. It is, of course, impossible for me without having a copy of the statement, which contains a number of features affecting the textile industry and other industries in this country, to comment on it objectively. I should prefer to wait until I see the text; then if there are statements to be made they can be made at the opportune time.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON VOLUNTARY CONTROLS ON EXPORTS TO CANADA
speechtext:
Our group is immensely pleased with the announcement which has been made. Over many years we have advocated planning between nations in respect to the exchange of commodities as opposed to raising tariff barriers. I am happy to note that this is a voluntary arrangement agreed to by the government of Japan. I hope the government intends to enlarge its activities in this field and enter into further understandings of this kind with other nations of the world in order that we may have an orderly economic life in our own nation without the upsets which are inevitably caused by ruthless competition in the world's trading field.
I noted particularly the expression of opinion by the minister at the conclusion of his observations to the effect that he was looking for an expansion of our trade with Japan. We hope his prediction in this respect will be realized. We need Japan as an active trading partner, and we believe there is room in Japan for the export industry of Canada. We hope that at no time will the

government revert to the old policy of using tariff barriers. We are happy with the new attitude which is being taken.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF FIRST OFFERING TO SECONDARY MORTGAGE MARKET

speakeroldname: Hon. D. J. Walker (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF FIRST OFFERING TO SECONDARY MORTGAGE MARKET
speechtext:
Hon. members may recall that on April 17 I announced that the government had directed Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to initiate the development of an active secondary market for National Housing Act residential first mortgages. This was to be accomplished by the sale of a part of the large and diversified portfolio the corporation has acquired as a result of extensive lending operations since 1957. In answer to several inquiries I agreed to make a further statement when the modus oper-andi had been worked out.
The corporation's first offering of National Housing Act insured mortgages will now be made on or about June 1. The initial offering, in an amount of approximately $15 million, will be made to members of the investment dealers' association of Canada, N.H.A. approved lenders and their N.H.A. approved correspondents. These organizations may then offer the mortgages for sale to pension funds, trusts, estates, holding companies and the public, or they may wish to hold the mortgages and offer debentures or other forms of security to small investors. Prospective purchasers should therefore get in touch with one of the organizations I have just mentioned, and not with the corporation itself.
The mortgages to be offered for sale in about two weeks time have been assembled in packages valued at about $500,000 each. Some packages consist of mortgages in specific centres; others have been prepared on a country wide basis. Each contains fully advanced 6| per cent N.H.A. first mortgages.
On or about June 1, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will invite sealed tenders from prospective purchasers and bids may be for one or more of the $500,000 mortgage packages up to the maximum of $15 million. Tender documents will be mailed by the corporation from its head office in Ottawa. I might add that options for up to 60 days will be considered. Tenders will close at 11 a.m. E.D.T. on June 19, 1961.
Secondary Mortgage Market
The corporation will not insist upon retaining the servicing. The purchasers of the mortgages may choose their own servicing arrangement. I should point out, however, that under provinsions of the National Housing Act an insured mortgage may be sold and the mortgage insurance continued only if it is administered to maturity by the corporation or by an approved lender.
No further sales will be made for a period of 60 days from the date of the original option.
Subsequent government marketing policy will be determined in light of the experience we gain from the first offering. I am confident, however, that development of an active secondary mortgage market will create not only a more regular but actually a larger flow of National Housing Act mortgage funds.
In concluding my statement may I reiterate that the sale of mortgages by C.M.H.C. does not in any way affect the interests of borrowers. These are established when the mortgage is made, and do not change when it is sold.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we on this side of the house welcome this announcement of the minister in regard to the establishment of a secondary mortgage. We believe, however, that this move is long overdue. It will be recalled that we recommended the establishment of such a market on many occasions over the past three year period. Anything that can be done to encourage a steadier flow of mortgage money into housing will surely be welcomed by all groups in this house. We have seen the difficulties and great hardships which have faced the house building industry and the public in general, at a time not later than the year 1960, resulting from this lack of a steady flow as well as from the necessity, at times, of the government turning on and off the tap.

Mr. Speaker, as indicated on another occasion, our group is heartily in accord with the plan of the government to establish what we hope will be a reliable secondary mortgage market in Canada. We feel this project will go a long way toward meeting the need for capital on the part of the house building industry.
I noted very carefully that the minister announced it was the government's intention to place-if I heard him correctly-only $15 million of the securities on the market. I believe this is a wise move indeed. I was afraid the government might have flooded the market with a much larger amount, because we do know the government holds $1J billion worth of mortgage paper.
I can assure the minister that we welcome the move, and that we will be watching very carefully the method of its operation and particularly the effects on the market of any undue unloading on the part of the government.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the announcement of the Minister of Public Works, are the chartered banks of Canada going to be permitted to submit bids on the blocks of mortgages referred to by the minister? If so, would this not be circumventing the intent of the Bank Act which limits the earnings of the banks?

speakeroldname: Hon. D. J. Walker (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF FIRST OFFERING TO SECONDARY MORTGAGE MARKET
speechtext:
The answer to the question is yes, but the banks would not be circumventing the Bank Act. The hon. member does not appear to appreciate that the banks can invest in securities yielding a greater rate of return than 6 per cent. With respect to lending to the public, and this is the distinction, the limit is 6 per cent. If the banks want to lend money on mortgages as approved lenders the rate is limited to 6 per cent. The Canadian government's position as presented to the first United Nations conference on the law of the sea in 1958, was to the effect that a state has a fishing zone contiguous to its territorial sea extending to a limit 12 nautical miles from the baseline from which the breadth of its territorial sea is measured in which it has the same rights in respect of fishing and the exploitation of the living resources of the sea as it has in its territorial sea.
The purpose of the bill is to extend the zone to a 12 mile area, which would then be the fishing zone, as distinct from the actual 3 mile zone. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my absence

Inquiries of the Ministry the hon. member for Port Arthur asked me the following question:
In view of press speculation and general criticism in many parts of the country, would the minister consider making a more specific and thorough statement on the matter of the information gained by census takers next month and its possible use for political purposes?
The answer is as follows. At every stage of their instructions the census enumerators are impressed with the confidential nature of their job. This action is in line with the first page of the enumeration manual, which contains the following instructions to the census takers:
You are not permitted to combine your census duties with any other work such as canvassing for personal gain or for political, church, or community organizations.
The law requires that all information collected for the census be kept confidential. You have taken an oath that you will not reveal any census information to anyone who is not a sworn census employee. To make sure you keep this oath, follow these rules:
(1)	Do not repeat any information you receive as an enumerator to anyone except census officials:
(2)	Do not leave completed census questionnaires where they can be seen by anyone except census officials;
(3)	Do not let anyone except census officials go with you on your visits;
(4)	Interview each respondent privately or with only members of his own family present. If necessary, explain that you are not supposed to get the information in the presence of anyone not employed in the census office.
Every census taker is required in section 6 of the Statistics Act to take and subscribe to the following oath:
I	 solemnly swear that I will faithfully and honestly fulfil my duties as (census enumerator) in conformity with the requirements of the Statistics Act and of all regulations thereunder, and that I will not, without due authority in that behalf, disclose or make known any matter or thing which comes to my knowledge by reason of my employment as such (census enumerator).
I can assure the house that the officials of my department have ben directed to ensure that these instructions and the safeguards provided to each individual Canadian by the Statistics Act are faithfully applied. Anyone found disclosing information for political or other purposes will be immediately prosecuted under section 34 of the Statistics Act. I am forwarding a copy of this statement to every census commissioner who has been appointed for the census next month.

At the time of adjournment last night, Mr. Chairman, I had touched on some of the subjects which I had discussed previously in connection with the C.N.R. I shall continue that discussion a little further. I intend to talk about the St. Lawrence seaway tolls after I get through speaking on these matters, if I have the time in which to do so. If not, I shall be obliged to take up the matter again at another opportunity and give others a chance to speak on the subject. However, I should like to finish my remarks if possible before the adjournment.
One matter that was mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver East was that of public ownership. I would go along with him in what he said. He pointed out that it seemed that only public ownership might make a success of anything. However, there are some cases in which it just does not happen. I know we have made a success of public ownership in Ontario in connection with

Supply-Transport
hydro and the development of power, and also in the city of Toronto in connection with our transportation. To date they have made an outstanding success in that regard. It is true that we have run into a little bit of difficulty in financing the subway. However, I am sure that public ownership, when it is handled in the right way, always results in outstanding success. Nevertheless I have found that when private enterprise cannot handle some matter or when it becomes a monopoly, the government generally takes it over.
In this case the government has taken over defunct railways of this country and given it to the Canadian National Railways to administer. So far the venture has not been an outstanding success. That is the reason for most of the comment that has taken place recently. People are not satisfied with the service that is given. I touched on that matter last night. The service has not been what it should be. Perhaps that is one of the reasons the undertaking has not been a success. There has been no attempt to make the service attractive. The convenience of the passengers or the people using the C.N.R. has been the last consideration.
I corroborate the statement made by the hon. member for Vancouver East with regard to reservations. You will be told that they are filled up and that you will have to wait. Then when you get on the train you find there is plenty of accommodation for you if they want to give it to you. I do not know where the fault lies. The board of directors is sufficiently large to take care of almost any incidental writing that needs to be taken care of. One would think this would be one of the things in which they would be vitally interested.
There is also the other matter that I mentioned with regard to stations. It occurs at both the union station in Toronto and the union station in Ottawa, which is one of the most deplorable of the stations. In fact it is not a union station any more either in Toronto or in Ottawa. These stations have just become glorified freight sheds. The convenience or service of the passengers is the last thing in which the railways are interested, in my opinion. Probably if they would smarten up they would find people willing to use their services. Probably they would like to use them. I do not mind paying for service, but I do not like paying for it when I do not get it.
As a matter of fact I can get home to Toronto from Ottawa more quickly by driving my car than I can by going by train. I might also say that not much time is saved in going by air, as far as I am concerned. These are things to cause one to ponder.

I refer particularly to the timetable. I do not ever remember arriving in Ottawa on the scheduled time in the morning. You are always late. I wonder what they do with the time during which they fool around down at Perth, Smiths Falls and the various other places, which could have been used in order to get them to the Ottawa station at the time indicated on the timetable.
Mention is made of the piggy-back service and of what a wonderful success it has been. That service is not anything new. It was being used on the Pacific coast from Seattle down to San Francisco and Los Angeles. It relieved the truck driver from having to make a tiresome drive. It gave him some rest. It was also done at a more economic rate. It is not something that is new. The situation is probably the same as it was when, if my memory serves me correctly, Sir Henry Thornton was head of the C.N.R. and Sir Edward Beatty was chairman of the C.P.R. The same thing applies here, I suppose. There was the time they lowered the rate from Toronto to Hamilton; it went down from something like $2.30 to $1.60 or $1.70. I can remember Tommy Church describing Sir Henry Thornton, the then president. He said, "It is the same thing; when the C.P.R. lowers the rates Sir Henry Thornton, as president of the C.N.R., just lowers their rates and follows along".
The same thing applies to the piggy-back. They have adopted what has been found to be successful with others. There is also the matter of trucking. I talked on this trucking matter with railroad men as far back as 1924. They had railway right of ways for running the trains, and the highways were not as large or as numerous then as they are now. They were running into trouble because the trucks were not making good time and I wondered why they could not use the railway right of way for putting trucks and goods on the railways. Then any time they wanted they could run the trucks off the railway right of way and onto any side road and have a good service. They said they would not be permitted to do that.
This was about 40 years ago, and they are just waking up now and getting into the trucking business. In those days these people were handling freight by horses and wagons, and only recently has there been a transition into trucking. They are just now getting around to going into the trucking business. They could have gone into it long ago. Now they are confronted with the vested rights of the trucking business, which are causing a lot of concern and they will find out that perhaps it is not going to be very successful or profitable for them.

Now I come to the question of the president of the Canadian National Railways. In the last two or three years there has been a lot of comment and a great deal of criticism in connection with the president. When you examine the matter you find that the president of the Canadian National Railways came to be on the board of directors because he had a nomination from the Bank of Canada. He took over, and there is some reason why he was sent to the railway, because he had made such a name during the war years in connection with the Bank of Canada and also, I think, with the wartime prices and trade organization. No one is trying to take away from the things he accomplished there; they were possibly good, but this did not mean he would be an outstanding railway man.
When he was appointed to the C.N.R. he was thought of as a wonderful individual who was going to accomplish great things for the Canadian National Railways. Because of his knowledge of banking and other things it was thought great things were going to take place in the C.N.R., but they did not take place. We have evidence that since he has been in office more things have not been accomplished than have been accomplished; we have more proof that he has not accomplished anything. He has not made the economies it was thought he would make, and what he has done since being appointed to the board is to practically truncate the service; he has reduced it. He can probably be called the great truncator of the Canadian National Railways.
This raises the question of the employees who are concerned. The employees of the railway are vitally concerned because this truncation has taken place on the railway. This matter was touched upon by the hon. member for Acadia last night when he mentioned the morale of the employees who were hired by the railway. Their morale is low, and perhaps rightly so, because they are in a better position to judge these matters than we are. They have probably come to the conclusion, and perhaps rightly so, that while he is the president and also a director, he is not in fact the manager of Canadian National Railways, but rather than being manager and director he is really the receiver the government has put in to fold up the railway. I think this is the thought that has got into their minds.
I would say that so far he has done a pretty good job of being the receiver of the railway, and the employees of C.N.R. have begun to look at it in this way. That is why their morale is low. There is no reason for high morale among the employees, because the president has not the respect of his employees and they have no confidence in him. He is not a railroad man; he is a banker.

Hon. members know the situation in regard to banks nowadays, and I should like to tell the committee the story about the man who went into a bank to get a loan. This man had good collateral and very good security, but times were something like they are now and banks would not loan money no matter what the security was. They were tight money days, as they are now. However, this man was a good customer of the bank and the banker did not want to offend him, so he talked about different subjects. Then he said, "Recently I had a serious illness. I had to lose an eye. I had to have an eye taken out and an artificial one put in, so I have a glass eye. I pride myself on the fact that this eye defies detection by anyone. No one can tell the difference between my glass eye and my good eye. I will bet you $10, if you want to take it up, that you cannot tell which is my glass eye". The man who wanted the loan said "I will take you up". The banker said, "Which is my glass eye?" The man said, "Your glass eye is the one that is on your left side". The banker said, "You are the first man who has ever been able to tell that by looking. How did you discover it?" "Well", the man said, "it was not too difficult on my part. I looked at your eyes and immediately said to myself that the glass eye was on the left side because it showed more warmth than your right eye".
That is the situation today with regard to the employees of the railway. They look upon this man as having no feeling for them, that he is just there in a receivership capacity, and that is probably what he is there for. They look upon him as being there to fold up the passenger services of this railway, when he was put forward as a man of such eminence. He has great eminence; I suppose he is one of the most powerful men of this country, because he is practically lord of this whole domain, as far as Canada is concerned, from the Pacific to the Atlantic and from the Arctic wastes to the United States border. He can go anywhere he likes. He is probably the second highest man in the country, perhaps even higher than the Governor General as far as salary is concerned. He issues his orders and no one can defy them. He is practically a law unto himself, something the same as the governor of the Bank of Canada. No one can question the right of this individual and his facilities for getting around the country at our expense, issuing great orders and doing great things. He even went to Ungava, Newfoundland, where he was investigating the narrow gauge up there to see if he could do something better for them

Supply-Transport
where the woods are small. I suppose he figured on getting great prestige up there and obtaining their support.
He puts in all this effort, but there are very few people that I know of, even on the opposition side, who stand up for him. Even on the Conservative side we find hon. members who will not stand up for him, and he is even losing the admiration of such hon. members as the hon. member for Greenwood, who has been a great admirer of his, and the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe, who in the committee said he was a wonderful fellow and it is probably a tough type of job that he has; it is just like shovelling fog or smoke. But he shovels a lot of other stuff besides smoke and fog that has a little more substance in it and is better used for fertilizer than smoke or fog. The hon. member for York North is also a great admirer of his. Why he is remains a mystery to me. He will probably explain it one day. He is an individual who wants to sell everything we have that is profitable and tells us to hang on to the things that are not profitable.
I should like to take a poll of this committee today, or any time we could have a free poll, and ask hon. members what they think of this great individual who has this country so tied up as far as the transportation system is concerned. I think you would find he would lose out by a 20 to 2 vote. The thing that remains for us to do is to be a little more concerned about the people of Canada and the transportation system, and take the necessary steps to see this system improved. We should get a person who is a railroad man, who would have the confidence of the railway employees. Donald Gordon does not have the confidence of anybody on the railway, I would say, even up in the higher echelon. It would be a good thing for this country if we got rid of the people who are causing the trouble.
There is another matter I should like to discuss at the present time. I will just touch upon it for the time being. I refer to the matter of grade level crossings. For years this matter has been advocated and we have been very successful in increasing the amount of the fund from $1 million up to $5 million, but still too many accidents take place year after year on our doorsteps. It has been increased until now it is $15 million a year. Even when this matter is tackled under the most favourable conditions we find that because of the method of financing, neither the railways nor the municipalities are able to make rapid progress in reducing these grade crossing tragedies. We shall probably have to devise a means of removing this responsibility from the shoulders of the municipalities and of the railways. As we all know, the

railways are running continually into deficits, and it is not very practical to ask them to attend to this matter of the removal of level crossings.
In Scarborough, which is in my own riding, there are 82 of these level crossings, possibly 90 of various descriptions. About 30 of them are on the fringe of being a menace to life. However, it happens occasionally that there is an accident off the beaten path, so these less used crossings cannot be entirely ignored. The local authority has taken care of one or two of these crossings in the past year, but they cannot go further; the provisions of the act as now applied do not allow them to deal with more than one or two a year. This work could be extended threefold throughout the Dominion of Canada if the present arrangements were reviewed and new steps were taken to deal with this menace which presents itself to road and rail traffic.
Last year the hon. member for High Park spoke on this subject and dealt with the formation of a Canada Council whose first president was Mr. Brooke Claxton. Later Mr. Ashe was president; I do not know who is president at the present time. The hon. member was concerned with all the accidents which happen on the highways of Canada generally. The figures he presented were astounding and appalling, so much so that the figures we have with regard to accidents at grade level crossings, high as they are, pale into insignificance compared with them.
The comparison does not lessen the gruesomeness of the tragedies which occur, but it does raise a larger question; because in the light of the total figures one cannot very well put on undue pressure for more to be done with regard to grade level crossings until the whole situation on Canadian highways and the rate of accidents generally have been taken into consideration. We have arrived at the point when statisticians are able to predict the number of road accidents and fatalities which will take place on certain days. These predictions almost always turn out to be correct, or very nearly so, and when a situation of that kind exists it is clear that something should be done to deal with it even if it means greatly increasing the preventive force.
Now I have dealt with that subject and I should like to turn to another matter. I see the hon. member for Laurier in his place, and I think he would probably be able to give me the information in which I am vitally interested. It concerns a subject which has been before the committee and the house on previous occasions. The hon. member for Laurier was, of course, minister of transport in the former administration at the time he was the hon. member for Stormont. Later

he became chairman of the authority itself. He has spoken on this subject on many occasions in this house, and in the course of his remarks has made some statements which I am not able to fathom. I am not questioning that what he says is right, but I found it hard to understand when he said there had been complete agreement by all parties with regard to the St. Lawrence seaway development. On the surface that appears to be correct. The hon. member went on to say that there had been no objection to the terms, no objection to the tolls being charged.

Mr. Chairman, I feel somewhat impelled to speak on this item at this time because of what I consider to be an unwarranted, unreasonable and unmerited attack made on the T.C.A. yesterday by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano. When in the interests of Canada this government or previous governments establish a policy and make provision for the financing of crown corporations and when those crown corporations prove successful, I fail to understand why attacks should be made upon them, and thereby attacks on policy of the government that took the action required, and why it is then said, "Let's get rid of it".
Let me give a brief illustration because, as I said, I cannot understand that kind of attack. A previous government, because of

necessity, established Polymer. A capital expenditure of $48,500,000 has returned over $100 million to the federal government. The government still owns a plant worth a maximum of $130 million, and now the cry is, "Let us hand this company over to the owners of free enterprise so that they can get their money out of it".
Who said that?
I would say two members from British Columbia.
Name them.
The hon. member for one.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member is misinterpreting and misrepresenting statements I made before the committee. The committee has not reported and I do not think the hon. member is in a position to discuss the matter at this particular time.

The investment of $9,500,000 in Eldorado has paid back $21 million and Canada still owns Eldorado.
Yesterday we heard, as I have said, an unwarranted, unreasonable and unmerited attack on the T.C.A. Without doubt, in an operation of the magnitude of T.C.A. all of us could find merited points of criticism. But, sir, I think such an attack on T.C.A. displays a deficient sense of responsibility. I acknowledge that the hon. member for Coast-Capil-ano was right; we have had a pioneering service in Canada which was established by our bush pilots in the northern territories of our country. But I challenge anyone to say that our bush pilots or free enterprise could in the 1930's have built anything to equal the Trans-Canada Air Lines system and an international airways system. That pioneering was done in 1937 with the establishment of the T.C.A. On an original investment of $5 million T.C.A. was formed.
A very safe investment.

Its first route was only 122 miles, and that was in British Columbia, Vancouver to Seattle. From 1937 until today this great pioneering endeavour, established by the public of Canada through the government, has expanded from 122 miles to an air route service of 30,399 miles. It has a domestic service in Canada and a service to the United Kingdom, to continental Europe and to the Caribbean covering, if my memory is correct, some 60 communities. This public service operation in Canada, which in those 30 years has expanded from the original 122 miles of service, as I have already pointed out, is now recognized as the seventh largest air carrier in the world and as one absolutely 90205-6-320

The criticism made yesterday by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano was on two grounds. First, he said that T.C.A. had a deficit of $2,607,000 last year. Admittedly it had a net deficit of $2,607,000 last year but those who now attack T.C.A. forget to mention that for the nine previous years it had surpluses. An attack is made on T.C.A. because it now requires an advance either from the C.N.R. or directly from parliament in the amount of $200 million in order to buy new equipment so that it may remain in the forefront and give leadership in air travel. The method of doing it.
What is wrong with that?
The method of doing it.

If C.P.A. wishes to make such an expenditure it has to get the money from the C.P.R., its controlling body. T.C.A. gets its money either from the C.N.R. or directly from parliament. I gathered that the hon. member for Coast-Capilano thought that this was wrong but he forgets that we subsidize the C.P.R. and have always subsidized it since there was a C.P.R.

I have a few remarks to make under this general item in the estimates of the Department of Transport, but first of all I should like to join with the other speakers in congratulating the Minister of Transport on the presentation of his first estimates and on the manner in which the department is being administered under his jurisdiction. When one looks at the eight pages of estimates in the blue book and sees that they cover marine services, railway and steamship services, air services including civil aviation, the meteorological branch, the St. Lawrence seaway authority, the air transport board and the board of transport commissioners, one gets some indication of the extent of the department's activities.
Comments on this item before us have ranged over nearly all the activities covered by the department. I will confine my remarks at this time to one subject that is of particular interest to many of my constituents, namely the lack of air service to my home city of Moose Jaw, Saskatchewan. I have spoken on this matter previously. I know the minister is familiar with the situation so I will make only brief comments at this time. Further details regarding the city's airport facilities are contained in letters sent to his department from time to time.
Moose Jaw actually pioneered air service in Saskatchewan, starting from a municipal air field on a flat piece of prairie grassland in the early 1920's. I well remember the start from this airfield of the first flight of the old western Canada air mail service to Edmonton. This was in the middle of the winter in 1927 or 1928, I believe. I was a passenger on that inaugural flight. In order to indicate

the great advances that have been made since that time, I might point out that the pilot was in an open cockpit in weather 30 degrees below zero.
Moose Jaw had the first air meet in the province in 1929 with planes coming in from many parts of Canada and the United States to put on an exhibition of stunt flying and parachute drops for a great crowd from all over southern Saskatchewan. Moose Jaw now has fine airport facilities in connection with the large R.C.A.F. station there. Up until May 6, 1959, the city had a scheduled commercial air service through Canadian Pacific Air Lines, and later through Pacific Western Airlines from Moose Jaw to Edmonton. Because of changes in the mail service, P.W.A. applied to the air transport board for permission to drop Moose Jaw from its flight schedule. I should like to quote one sentence from a letter received from Mayor O. B. Fysh of Moose Jaw as follows:
We are a city of 33,000 people, very much air minded, but having no air connections at all at the present time.
When T.C.A. established what is called the milk run, which takes in most prairie cities between Winnipeg and Calgary, Moose Jaw was not included although several smaller cities are serviced. As a member of the sessional committee which inquires into the annual report of T.C.A. I have presented Moose Jaw's arguments for air service on more than one occasion.
I have a letter from Mr. Gordon McGregor, president of T.C.A., commenting on the views I expressed at last year's committee meeting. He expresses the hope that at some time a satisfactory solution might be worked out.
It would appear, Mr. Chairman, that the time for a satisfactory solution is near at hand. According to reports, T.C.A. would like some other air line to take over the western milk run. Such a change will of course necessitate a public hearing.
My reason for speaking at this time is to ask the minister to make it possible for Moose Jaw to present its case at this hearing, to show that there could be sufficient passenger and air express business there to warrant a daily air service. There are new businesses in the city which could make use of air deliveries. A newly established greenhouse industry is now operating on a large commercial scale and no doubt could make large air shipments of cut flowers daily.
I do not believe the date has been set for a hearing on any possible change of service. When a hearing is arranged I hope that all interested parties will be able to attend. I hope the minister can give some assurance that this will be the case.

Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to speak at any length, nor do I propose to join in the debate which has taken place between hon. members from the province of British Columbia. Thus far that is a fight they have preferred to restrict to themselves and I think any intervention at this time would be most unproductive and unwise.
However, Mr. Chairman, I rise to discuss a matter that is of great interest to the county from which I come, and particularly to the city of Windsor. I do so at this time because it is the first opportunity I have had since the minister took over the administration of the Department of Transport of bringing to his attention a matter which we discussed last year during the presentation of a bill providing for the management and development of the harbour in the city of Windsor, and a companion bill for the same purpose for the city of Oshawa.
As the minister knows, there are under his jurisdiction, as I understand it, three types of harbour commissions. One type, I think, runs into pretty large figures. That is the type of harbour commission which now exists and operates in the city of Windsor, and which has operated for some time in the city of Hamilton, in the city of Toronto, in Belleville and now in Port Arthur and the city of Oshawa.
The harbour commission bill setting up a harbour commission in Windsor was introduced in this house by the former minister of transport, the Hon. George Marler. Last year the present administration-as I noted a moment ago-brought forward a bill providing for the management and development of the harbours in the cities of Windsor and Oshawa.
I should like the minister to take advantage at the earliest opportunity to come to Windsor. I hope he will come not just before an election, but long before, if there is to be a long interval, so that he can acquaint himself with the potential value that could flow from the development of the harbour in the city of Windsor.
The minister will be warmly welcomed and I hope I will have an opportunity, together with my two colleagues from the county of Essex, to make the minister's visit not only agreeable but informative and, having in mind my immediate purpose, highly educational.
The harbour commission in Windsor is in the early stages of existence and I want to make a plea today to the minister for a greater interest on the part of the Department of Transport, in particular, in its operations.
Supply-Transport
The city of Windsor is situated along some wonderful bodies of water; contiguous is lake St. Clair, the Detroit river, and nearby is lake Erie. We are right in the heartland of Canada's great waterway system and now, with the development of the St. Lawrence seaway, our community, like many others, looks for a development from the St. Lawrence project which will add to the economic richness of the area.
One of the means by which that can be effected is through efficient administration of local harbour commissions such as the one in the city of Windsor. We there have three commissioners. They are all public-spirited men, but I believe they need assistance. They must, of course, provide assistance themselves, but they also need assistance from that agency of government which is responsible for their creation and much of their direction.
I do not believe it is wise to take the position that we must wait until there is more water traffic and more use of the harbour facilities to put forward a plea for greater interest, financial and otherwise, on the part of the central government.
I remember last year when we discussed this matter the hon. member for Greenwood participated in the debate. He complained about the reliance, seemingly, that was being placed on the central government by local bodies such as the one on whose behalf I was then speaking. I fully appreciate that every community must play its part in the development of operations of this kind. There is undoubtedly a local interest, but there is also a national interest. When one thinks of the assistance given by federal governments to the ports of Toronto and Hamilton I think one is justified in asking for a greater interest on the part of the federal government.
At the present time some of these large ports, such as	in the city	of	Toronto, havebeen able to	develop	so	as	to	afford tosend scouts into other cities for business. Some of these new commissions and some of the communities in which these new commissions operate are not in that happy revenue position.	I think	that	at	this time,when we are	seeking	to	bring	about the
greatest possible economic development for our country, we should recognize that one way by which this can be done is by assisting local bodies.
If the federal government has the responsibility in law, as it has, for the nomination of harbour commissions and for the creation, indeed, under the law of a harbour commission, it seems to me it has a responsibility way beyond the mere act of creation and nomination of administrative personnel. I know that requests have been made of the minister-I do not know whether I can say

Supply-Transport
that of the present minister, but with regard to his predecessor that is certain-and the government for financial assistance.
I know that the economics division of the Department of Transport, particularly that section which concerns itself with harbours administration, has looked into the economic potential of the harbour commission on whose behalf I speak. Their reports are available for the minister to study. The minister has, I believe, received requests by the harbour commission for assistance, financial and otherwise and I believe those requests deserve to be supported. That is why I am rising again on the occasion on which the minister presents his estimates for the first time to ask him to tell us at the appropriate moment in our discussion what the present policy of the government is in regard to harbour commissions of this type. I suggest to the minister that if we just wait for such time as more adequate and extensive use is made of these harbours we shall be postponing unnecessarily much business which X think could be available if we were to establish the necessary foundations. That requires some promotion work. That requires some advertising. That requires the building of certain facilities. A project of this sort should, I think, be assisted by the federal government. I suggest to the minister this is a matter about which he should be in a position to say something today.
Now is the time to do this, because right opposite Windsor there is a development taking place in the city of Detroit which I think should encourage us to take similar action on the Canadian side. The development which is going on in the development of harbour facilities both in Detroit and all along the great lakes in the United States is such that if we are to be able to capture as much of this business as is open to us as a result of the operation of the St. Lawrence seaway we should act with prudent haste. The minister will recognize, I hope, that the area from which I come does offer a very special opportunity for the development of the community and the county in which the city of Windsor is situated.
There is an added reason for urging the minister to give some attention to this situation. We are handicapped in our section of the country by an unfair freight rate structure which operates against us. It is possible, for instance, to ship a bushel of grain from Chicago to Montreal cheaper than it is to ship a bushel of grain from Windsor to Montreal. Our freight rates are, generally speaking 25 per cent higher than the rates which prevail in the Toronto area. The city of Toronto has become a great distributing centre. Many industries are locating there

because it is such an important centre of distribution and we are unfairly affected in our competition because of this freight rate structure. The advantage of water transportation will reduce the effect of unfair and discriminatory freight rates which do exist, in the event that the royal commission does not provide a satisfactory answer. This is an additional reason for seeing to it that the local harbour commission is given the fullest co-operation, the fullest encouragement and the greatest possible financial assistance to undertake these operations at this time-not tomorrow, not in the long run, but today, so that we may be in the best position possible to take advantage of the business which undoubtedly is there if we go after it.
I know that the local commission, the local citizens, must take the initiative. But it is an initiative which must be supported by the federal Department of Transport; otherwise there would not have been the decision made in the first place to establish a commission in 1956. So I ask the minister to look into this situation. Perhaps at some appropriate moment he would make the kind of comment which would please me or at any rate make the kind of comment he thinks is warranted in the circumstances.
When he does that he might take into consideration a decision reached by a committee of this house-a committee to which reference was made by my friend the hon. member for Laurier. That committee unanimously urged the fullest examination by way of economic survey of the potential available in areas served by harbour commissions such as the one I have mentioned. I do not know what is the present position of this over-all survey but it would seem to me that such a survey, together with the examination which has been made by the economics division, would reveal that I am not exaggerating when I say that there is much business available for a harbour such as that of the city of Windsor, ideally located as it is on rich waters-waters now witnessing the transportation of goods which mark the buoyant economy we want to see Canada possess, particularly in view of the activity that is taking place right across the river.
Harbour facilities in Detroit will be taxed. It will not be possible in time, with the economic power of that city, to take full advantage of the facilities which are being provided there. There will have to be some alternative provided, and that place could easily and should be the harbour at Windsor. This is something which requires vision. I know, as I said a moment ago, that vision must exist on the part of the city of Windsor. That vision does exist today. I assure the

hon. gentleman that there is a desire to promote harbour development, particularly at this time. But I do believe greater interest is necessary on the part of the federal government and I hope the Minister of Transport will have some very good news for the city of Windsor when he speaks later in connection with this matter.
