Mr. Chairman, I rise this afternoon for the purpose of discussing, among other things, the activities of the Canadian National Railways in my constituency, and in particular, the application made by the officials of the Canadian National Railways to discontinue commuter train service in the eastern section of York-Scarborough. Last year officials of the Canadian National Railways appeared before a committee of this house and requested $100 million to construct a marshalling yard with by-pass routes through the north section of the Toronto area. The officials suggested, as one of the reasons for coming to this committee of parliament seeking $100 million, that the construction of this marshalling yard and by-pass route would solve the congestion problem which has occurred in the downtown and waterfront areas in the city of Toronto. They intended to clear that congestion by providing a feeder line similar to the spokes of a wheel, from the perimeter of Toronto to the centre of Toronto.
In answer to questions asked by myself and other hon. members of that committee, those officials suggested that with the establishment of this $100 million marshalling yard and by-pass route, the major impediment to the effective operation of commuter trains between the outskirts of Toronto and the downtown area would be removed. It was explained that the building of this bypass was of vital concern to these areas.
After every possible alternative route had been considered, it was decided that the only practical route was through the quiet, sleepy village of Thornhill in the north section of my constituency. The inhabitants of that village had established themselves there in an attempt to avoid the hustle, bustle and accompanying disturbances of big city business and traffic. However, they found themselves, following this decision, faced with the prospect of having a two line, 60 train per day freight route through the middle of the village. I am sure hon. members will appreciate that the inhabitants of that village were not wildly enthusiastic about that prospect. Perhaps I should repeat that this route was decided upon after each and every alternative had been considered exhaustively but reluctantly rejected.
Those officials came to that parliamentary committee requesting $100 million for the construction of these proposed projects, holding out as an inducement, the continuation and extension of commuter service in that area. I do not know whether the responsibility can be laid at the feet of the president of the Canadian National Railways, but someone in

Supply-Transport
the executive of that crown corporation should receive first prize for having the nerve of a canal horse, having come to this parliament offering the continuation of commuter service in exchange for $100 million and after two months making the decision to eliminate existing commuter services. I refer, of course, to the application which has been made in respect of Canadian National train No. 94. The reaction of the residents of Agincourt and Markham has been tremendous. A special meeting was held between the officials of the railroad and interested parties in that area. I attended that meeting as well. As a result of representations made at that time a tentative decision was reached, to discontinue the train service beyond the bounds of the Toronto limits and to retain the essential portion of the commuter service.
The metropolitan council of the city of Toronto has formed a committee with terms of reference to examine transportation problems generally in the city of Toronto, and to evaluate the necessity of commuter trains. It is my understanding this committee will also consider the cost and possibility of subsidizing these commuter services.
There has been some discussion during the consideration of this item regarding the degree of interest held by the officials of this railroad to passenger and commuter traffic. I have come to the conclusion that the railways officials would rather have their cars filled with cattle than human beings. I know of the existence of a society for the prevention of cruelty to animals but am not aware of a similar society in respect to human beings. I would suggest there should be such an organization in order to prevent some of the things which people are subjected to while travelling on the railways.
If it were my contention that the railway officials were intentionally trying to drive passengers away, I would suggest as an example, that hon. members consider the type and quality of food being served to passengers. In my opinion that represents one ingredient of this plot. The sandwiches now being dispensed by the express agent on these trains are priced at 35 cents. These sandwiches consist of two pieces of bread, ingeniously designed to turn into lumps of lead after being swallowed, covered with a microscopic film of what appears to be lard but what is probably uncoloured margarine, and a piece of the most tired rat cheese it has ever been my misfortune to attempt to consume. I use the words "attempt to consume" advisedly. I have been chewing on these sandwiches for some years now and I have never finished one yet.
I have discussed the situation with several of my colleagues and have arrived at the

conclusion that the cost involved in producing these sandwiches for sale on trains would not exceed 5 cents unless there was some formula involved in the making of the bread so that it will turn into lead. As I say, these sandwiches cost 5 cents to produce and are sold for 35 cents. One can of course purchase the ham variety of sandwich which is about as pleasurable and delightful to eat as an old piece of shoe leather.
I should like the minister to investigate this situation and inform the committee why these express agents are allowed to perpetrate what can only be described as a fraud against the travelling public of Canada. If a contract exists between the railways and the express agents allowing them to sell this outrageous product at an even more outrageous price, could the minister tell us when the contract will come up for renewal so that some form of control can be applied, or something can be done to correct this particular situation.
As I started to say, it would seem at times that there is a plot within the railway system to discourage passenger traffic. My hon. friend from Danforth has expressed opinions and related experiences concerning the relationship of passengers to baggage. Anybody travelling between Ottawa and Toronto and stopping at Leaside or at other stations along the way, and at the station here, of course finds the trains made up in such a way that when they arrive at the station and it is time for the passengers to disembark the baggage and the baggage handling get first preference. At times one has to walk for the better part of half a mile, part of it through cinders, and perhaps in the rain, on wet concrete the rest of the way to reach the station platform. There you will find the baggage handlers in dry comfort unloading their portion of the train. This is the attitude toward passenger traffic. It seems to me no imagination has been used in the provision of passenger comfort. People are discouraged from travelling on trains. As soon as the number of passengers declines the railways go before the board of transport commissioners and apply to have the passenger service dropped entirely. It is a very easy way to avoid one's responsibilities.
Another question that came up when the officials of the C.N.R. were present at Agincourt to determine the feelings of the community was that of advertising. It is my understanding that the C.N.R. spends some $2 million in general advertising. Some of that advertising abroad probably has a residual benefit in encouraging people to visit Canada. It seems to me, if you are going to operate an efficient passenger service and an efficient commuter passenger service the first

thing that an intelligent, reasonable man would do would be to approach the people in the area already concerned who are using the commuter trains and encourage them to extend their use of the trains; to do some advertising in the local newspapers and make some positive effort to encourage a greater use of the commuter trains.
They argue that the number of commuter cars do not justify the use of an engine. Obviously, if you want more passengers you are going to have to tell the potential customers about the service that is available, and make a great effort to convince those people that they should use the commuter trains. At no time have I seen in the local newspapers any advertisement of any description other than some general advertising proclaiming some great service such as "Travel with your family on trains". I could spend the next half hour describing some of the experiences I have had with my own family in travelling on trains, but perhaps that would not be quite to the point. The point is, Mr. Chairman, no real effort is made anywhere to examine the passenger structure in this country, to improve the service or to encourage people who would normally use the passenger service to use it to a greater extent.
I would hope that the C.N.R. would continue to operate the commuter trains which they have said would remain in the service. I would hope they would do everything they can to accommodate the timetables and schedules on the trains to the convenience of the passengers, and to encourage more passengers to use the trains. I would hope they would spend some of the $2 million in placing advertisements either in the local newspapers or in some other media to encourage people in the area to make full use of the commuter trains.
The congestion of traffic in Toronto, as in other major cities, is a difficult problem. We have a major through way program and an expressway program under way at the present time. We are embarking on an extended subway program, but still the most efficient, effective and fastest method of transportation from the perimeter to the centre of Toronto is over the existing rights of way. I would suggest further that some attempt be made to design a cheaper commuter car. Normally, those trains will not be travelling at the great speeds at which the passenger trains would be travelling. It seems to me, therefore, there should be some saving in the weight and in the solidity of the structure which would not be specifically exposed to any of the hazards of a trans-continental train which travels at speeds up to 80 and 90 miles an hour.
Supply-Transport
These are some of the suggestions that I would hope the minister would keep in mind in his consultations with the Canadian National Railways. I would hope that, with the co-operation of the Canadian National, the Canadian Pacific and metro Toronto, we can look forward to the day in that city when an efficient, effective pattern of commuter service will be serving the people.

After the friendly exchange between the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis) and the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville (Mr. Johnson) I thought I should rise myself on that matter of canalization.
Yesterday, the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville seemed to think that the most important aspect in the matter of the Richelieu seaway project was that it should pay its way. Anyway, as the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville said, this matter also seemed vital to the minister because he stated that the project was not economically sound.
Now, I wonder what is meant exactly by an economically sound project? Does it mean only the immediate revenue from the passage of ships through the locks or elsewhere, or is the economic development which such canalization may entail taken into account?
The matter I want to deal with has been under consideration for years. It is the Ottawa seaway project.
We were discussing that even before the ' St. Lawrence seaway development, but I can quite understand why this Ottawa river scheme was set aside as a secondary project, if it is compared to the other.
However, I think deepening those waterways, both the Ottawa and the Richelieu, would tend to develop and decentralize some industries which, today, as everyone agrees, are too centralized in one community or an other. Furthermore, is it not a fact that the economic development of one or two areas would be well worth the expense required of the government to bring prosperity outside Canada's larger centres.
I think at the present time, there would be something to be gained in deepening both rivers at the same time. In my constituency, there are pulp and paper companies exporting rather large quantities across the border, where the New York market is considered most important. If the Ottawa and Richelieu rivers were deepened, it would reduce the distance by some 1,200 miles for those products.

Supply-Transport
If we consider that waterway transport is much less expensive than railway transport, this would allow our pulp and paper companies to compete with the European continent companies which have a kind of wood somewhat like the one in the province of Quebec, however, these companies can manufacture and sell their paper cheaper, for while transportation costs from Europe to the United States are expensive enough, European paper mills still have an advantage on ours.
However, if we had the advantages of both these seaways, we could see pulp and paper mills develop along the Ottawa river, for we are not short of power-we have it-and we could find the necessary labour, but what we lack are means of transportation.
As a matter of fact, on the Quebec side, we only have the Canadian Pacific, and if we want to use the Canadian National, we have to cross over to Ontario. Furthermore, transportation rates are increasing all the time. It could hardly be otherwise, since the administration costs of railways have increased and, on account of that, they have to find revenues from all quarters in order to have both ends meet.
That is a real difficulty, but we must not, on account of the expenses of our railways, allow our industries to sutler to the extent of losing certain foreign markets which we are entitled to nave.
That is why I think the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville was right when he said that the department should undertake at once a serious study of all those projects, because such a study requires researches in all fields, which means lots of work and time. If we lose time before undertaking such a study, where shall we stand?
Besides, on the matter of economic soundness, I should like to refer to a quotation made yesterday by the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville, which supports precisely my argument. It is part of a thesis submitted to the University of Syracuse by a Mr. Tefft who states the following:
Finally, I do not think that the ultimate decision as to whether or not the waterway should he deepened and, ii so, to what depth, should be overly influenced by cost-benefit ratios. I do not deny the usefulness of ratios, but a dollar and cent sign cannot possibly be hung on the defence value of an improved waterway.
Then too, I am struck with the highly problematical nature of benefit estimates. They cannot accurately take into account the future, if for no other reason than that they do not know what it will be. This is particularly true in a region that appears to be about to undergo the unusually rapid change that seems to be in store for the Champlain basin.

We also hope that the Department of Transport will favourably consider the deepening of the Ottawa river, for we can forecast in our area an industrial development that will employ all the available working force, and this would help our people a great deal.
Even though we know that we will not cover the cost of the project in one, 10 or even 20 years, we should not forget that the industrial development that would take place would yield taxes to the government; it would produce transport income which, in turn, yields taxes to the government.
It seems to us that, even if the project should not prove to be a profitable one as far as revenues from the waterway itself are concerned, there would be a certain degree of profit because of the indirect revenues that the government would derive from the industrial development of the area.
I therefore ask the minister to seek information from the experts of his department, to ascertain the possibilities of the development of these waterways.
The deepening of the Ottawa river would go hand in hand with the deepening of the Richelieu river. I think those projects would complement each other.
If they could be implemented, I am sure that, as a consequence, two important areas in the country would experience the expansion they are entitled to and we would have only congratulations and thanks to extend to the government.

Mr. Chairman, I want to say just a few words about Canadian Pacific Air Lines and Trans-Canada Air Lines. The hon. member for Vancouver East gave T.C.A. quite a boost. He went into rhapsodies about it. In the part of the country from which I come we would be walking or riding horseback if we did not have C.P.A. A railroad runs in there but the train only operates a couple of times a week or maybe once a week or maybe not at all. There is a sleeper on the train but you have to put a blanket across the window to keep the wind out.
C.P.A. really serves the north country. When we go home we land at Fort St. John. If we were waiting for T.C.A. we would still be in Edmonton. T.C.A. does not allow C.P.A. to pick up passengers who are going toward Toronto. T.C.A. insists on taking all such passengers from Whitehorse, the Yukon, Fort St. John, Prince George and that region.

C.P.A. renders a real service to the north and it is the north in which I am interested.
Canadian Pacific Air Lines and Trans-Canada Air Lines are two really good air lines. I was down in Kentucky on the 6th of May.
What were you doing?

I was at a church meeting. There is no comparison between C.P.A. and T.C.A. on the one hand and Eastern Air Lines on which I travelled. The employees are not interested in the passengers. I thought the girl on the plane had had a battle with her husband, if she had one, because she was so sour. But the personnel at the airports are excellent. I have never had better service from anybody.
When I came back from the race track to Louisville I told the fellow I wanted to get back to Ottawa. This was Saturday night at eight o'clock. He said, "Come on over and meet the boss". The boss turned out to be the head man at the Louisville airport. He said, "Where do you want to go"? I said, "Ottawa". He said, "I will get you there. I will have you in New York tonight." I said. "I do not want to go to New York". He said, "We will fly you to Columbus and then to Cleveland and then to Toronto". I was here next morning at eleven o'clock. That is service.
In time for church.

I think T.C.A. is giving C.P.A. a rough deal. I know Mr. McConachie, the president of C.P.A., personally. He lived at Fort St. John for four years. He was a bush pilot. If some Eskimo or Indian child or one of our own children was sick, he would fly them out no matter what the weather was like. He was a real credit to the north. I should like to see him get a break so that C.P.A. can have other routes across Canada.
T.C.A. gets all the breaks. They can fly to London. The British government will let Mr. McConachie's air line land in London but T.C.A. will not allow it. I am not too well versed in these matters. C.P.A. has to go to Amsterdam. Why can they not have the right to land at London, England? I understand the British authorities have given them permission to land there. The Minister of Transport can tell us all about it. On the west coast C.P.A. is losing passengers to another line running down to Seattle. Everybody goes that way and C.P.A. cannot have that route.
It was only a short time ago that T.C.A. were trying to make a deal with an air line from Japan. I think that C.P.A. should get a break in this deal. They are Canadians. It is true that the hon. member for Vancouver East attempted to "blow up" T.C.A. However, these people are also Canadians and they pay
Supply-Transport
taxes. Speaking of paying taxes, all we do is to pay taxes to Mr. McGregor's outfit. May I say that I am not against T.C.A. However,
I should like to see these other people get a break. If you are going across the ocean now via B.O.A.C., what do you find? You find that they are flying with the cheap propeller driven planes. T.C.A. do not use them. They do not have this kind. They are much higher than that. However, B.O.A.C. have them. I do not think C.P.A. are getting the break which they should get.

speechtext:
I do not want to take up the time of the committee unduly but there are one or two reasons why I desire to intervene at this stage. The first is to deal with some questions that were addressed to myself during the course of this discussion and also to say something in connection with what transpired yesterday when the hon. member for Coast-Capilano entered the discussion in connection with something I had said concerning T.C.A. and the air policy of the government. I did not take as seriously as did the hon. member for Vancouver East the statements made by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano. I thought that they were fair criticism. While I do not agree with him in many of the things he said, I rise to make a statement in connection with the matter. I have risen, Mr. Chairman, not to defend T.C.A. I think that is the responsibility of the minister. I think the minister is responsible to parliament for Trans-Canada Air Lines in the same manner as he is responsible for the Canadian National Railways. If he follows the practice which has been followed in the past and which most ministers of transport have followed, he will give the picture as it is related to him by the responsible officers of both those crown corporations. There is, of course, the committee in which members can examine the officers that come there from time to time.
I am rising chiefly to point out that under the former administration we were determined to prevent from arising a situation such as that which arose under the Borden government with railways when too many trans-continental lines were built and none of them could pay. I do not think there can be any challenge to that statement. As the committee knows, Mr. Borden had to bail out Mackenzie and Mann for $10 million which was a great deal of money in those days. In this whole picture of trans-continental air lines policy, the government should make sure not to distribute the transcontinental air lines in such a manner that neither company can make money and that the treasury will have to foot the bill. That is what the MacPherson commission is doing

Supply-Transport
at the present time with the railways. I hope it will not happen with the air lines. Perhaps the hon. member for Greenwood will remember that $10 million. As the hon. member said, all I am suggesting is that we should apply common sense to this policy. I refer to the policy of the government. If we do that, then I think we will arrive at a proper conclusion.
I want to make some reference to the speech made by the hon. member for Van-couver-Kingsway. I am sorry that he is not in his seat.
Keep it going; I will be right back.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
It was, I must say at once, a remarkable speech and I wish to commend that hon. member not only for the knowledge which he possesses of the freight rate question but for the objective manner in which he spoke on this subject. It has been a long time since I heard a speech on freight rates of that calibre in this chamber. I am not saying that I agree with what he said. However, I am saying that he rose to deal objectively with the subject of freight rates. For instance, he pointed to a matter that has caused a great deal of concern to the former administration. It has to do with the one and one third rule and the agreed charges. I refer to the one and one third rule which was recommended by the Tur-geon royal commission on transportation. The agreed charges which amended the Transport Act, according to the province of Alberta, annulled the benefits of the one and one third rule. About the time at which I left the government there was a great deal of opposition to the effect of the amendment of the Transport Act on the one and one third rule. That was why it was necessary to call in the Turgeon commission again and to have it make a report such as the one it made.
The hon. member said another thing with which I am fully in agreement. I note that the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway is now in his seat. I am sorry he was not here earlier but I do not think he could have found any fault with what I said concerning his contribution. The other thing on which I agree fully with him is this. He said, "This is not a political question". There could be no greater truism than that. Freight rates are not and should not be a political question. I am sorry the hon. member was not here when I sat on the other side of the house in the place occupied by the present Minister of Transport and in a position to observe the kind of attitude the opposition took in this chamber. I made it quite clear that freight rates were effected by the board of transport commissioners and not 
by the cabinet or the government and that the board of transport commissioners was established for that purpose. But do you think the opposition listened to me? They did not listen to me in the slightest degree. From those who were interested to those who sit on our right now came the attack and the charge that we were the ones who were responsible for allowing these horizontal rates to increase unjustly from one end of the country to the other.
There was only once-and by once I mean during one period of time-in the long history from confederation down to the present time when the government was responsible for the establishment of freight rates and that was when the cabinet itself dealt with them. The cabinet used to deal with freight rates-just imagine that situation-across Canada. That power was taken away-and rightly so-from the cabinet and was put into the hands of the board of transport commissioners. Of course, if I have made the statements which I made earlier, I have done so as a result of the statements made by the Prime Minister during the campaigns of 1957 and 1958 when he went from one end of the country to the other and said, on freight rates, "Did we act? Of course we acted. Here is what we did". That is nothing but an invitation to political attacks.
The freight rate question is a highly complex and complicated matter which should be left to a technical board such as the board of transport commissioners.
I pass on to another matter which was raised by the hon. member for Danforth in connection with the St. Lawrence seaway tolls. I suppose that if I wanted to take the proper attitude I would say to the hon. member that the Minister of Transport is in his seat and the questions which the hon. member directed to me should be directed to the minister because he is now responsible for the administration of that body and I am not.
However, I will not take that attitude. The hon. member said, "Why was there no opposition to the question of tolls? No mention was made of tolls on the Welland canal". Perhaps I should say to the hon. member that under the 1932 treaty there was no question of tolls, and the situation was the same under the 1941 agreement, both of which, as the hon. member rightly said, were not ratified by the congress of the United States.
Then, because of the many delays occurring in the United States and Canada, there arose a great desire on the part of both countries to find a solution to this problem and to bring about the project. The solution was found by means of a joint application on the

part of Canada and the United States to the international joint commission whereby, if that application were successful, legislation would be introduced by Canada for the construction of the seaway.
That legislation was introduced in 1951 by the act known as 15-16 George VI, an act to establish the St. Lawrence seaway authority. So there may be no doubt in the mind of my hon. friend, who seems to think there was no authority for these tolls, I would point out that the authority is set out in the act of parliament just as clearly as it could be.
In the first place let me say that earlier Canada had decided to deepen the St. Lawrence waterway up to Montreal at a cost of about $100 million, payable by the taxpayers of Canada. Canada had also decided to deepen the new Welland canal at a cost of about $132 million, payable by the taxpayers of Canada, on both of which there were no tolls. On the other hand the United States had agreed to carry out the deepening of the connecting channels, which would cost about $100 million.
This act was introduced in 1951 and section 10 clearly sets out what were the purposes and powers of the authority. They were, first, to build a deep-sea waterway between the port of Montreal and lake Erie, which included the Welland canal; and next, to construct, maintain and operate all such works as were necessary for that purpose.
If we look at section 17 we find these words:
Where the works have been constructed and are maintained and operated by the authority to provide, in conjunction with works undertaken by an appropriate authority in the United States, the deep waterway mentioned in section ten,-
That is the section I have referred to:
-tolls may be established pursuant to sections fifteen and sixteen or by agreement between Canada and the United States-
We were defeated in 1957, after this legislation was passed, of course, but before- and long before-the agreement referred to herein had been made between Canada and the United States. I am not suggesting for a moment that the government should have repudiated this section, but I am stating that it was after 1957 that the international tolls-making committee was established; it was after 1957 that the former minister of transport, the present Minister of Trade and Commerce, placed on the table the order in council which established the agreement and the tolls on both the St. Lawrence and Welland canals.
My hon. friend says, "The agreements were made between the two authorities, one from the United States and the other from
Supply-Transport
Canada. The question is: why was the cost not absorbed by the government itself, as was done in the United States with respect to the three rivers I have mentioned?"
I am afraid that question will have to be directed to the present Minister of Transport because that was done during the regime of the present government. But in so far as the former government was concerned, I must say that it would not have been possible to obtain the consent of the government of the United States unless those tolls had been imposed.
The reason we accepted the imposition of tolls was because we felt it was only fair that the users should pay for the canal, and not the taxpayers of Canada. The people of British Columbia and the Atlantic provinces would have opposed the seaway, and rightly so, if they had been expected to pay for it out of their taxes.
I remember that when this matter was discussed in the House of Commons there was unanimity. Hon. members from the Atlantic provinces said, "We fear this may be of some hurt to us, but we have come to the conclusion that this is a good thing for Canada. We have come to the conclusion that anything that helps one part will help the whole, and we will therefore support it on that basis".
I think, too, there was the other reason which I have just mentioned, namely that if we had not made this a toll seaway it would not have been possible to obtain unanimity from all parts of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I now wish to consider another question.
Yesterday, we had a debate on the deepening of the Richelieu river. The hon. member for Chambly-Rouville (Mr. Johnson) who took part in the debate asked me certain questions, particularly why the member for Laurier, either as minister of transport or as president of the St. Lawrence seaway authority had not considered the possibility of deepening the Richelieu river. He also asked me why the member for Laurier, at the time he was either minister of transport or the chairman of the seaway authority, had paid absolutely no attention to the the Richelieu waterway.
Mr. Chairman, the answer is quite simple. In fact, if the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville had referred to the reports, or if he only had studied the act, he would not have asked that question. On the other hand, had he read the book he mentioned last night, he would also have found out that the answer to his question is given there in two parts.
As for my responsibility as minister of transport, I never had the opportunity of

Supply-Transport
studying the possibility of deepening the Richelieu, for a reason that is found in a preliminary report prepared by the boundary waters commission.
That commission in fact had been called upon, in 1937, to make a survey concerning the possible dredging of the Richelieu, and had submitted a rather lengthy report dealing with all aspects of the matter, that is: the five routes, specifications concerning the seaway, whether the channel should be 14 or 27 feet deep, its cost, the volume of traffic, etc. The commission arrived at the following conclusion which I read from the preliminary report:
The commission recommends that this report be considered as a preliminary report and that the commission be authorized to maintain its jurisdiction over that question until the St. Lawrence seaway project is completed, and that the commission be given the opportunity to study the impact of its operation on the Richelieu seaway project.
Now, Mr. Chairman, it is obvious that as long as the St. Lawrence seaway was not completed, it surely was not proper for the government, in view of the decision of the boundary waters commission, to consider looking into that project.
In addition, the hon. member has asked me how it was that at the time I was chairman of the St. Lawrence seaway authority, I did not request our engineers and my officials to study the matter. The answer is quite simple. It is found in section 10 of the St. Lawrence seaway authority act. That section is as follows:
The authority is incorporated-
Why?
(a) acquiring lands for and constructing, maintaining and operating all such works as may be necessary to provide and maintain, either wholly on Canada or in conjunction with works undertaken by an appropriate authority in the United States, a deep waterway between the port of Montreal and lake Erie-
Such, Mr. Chairman, were the powers vested in the authority, namely the power of constructing a canal between the port of Montreal and lake Erie, and there was no intention of the power to consider the possibilities of the Richelieu waterway project. If we had considered anything else besides the St. Lawrence seaway, we would have abused our powers, which would have been illegal.
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member for Laurier permit a question?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Certainly.
Can the hon. member tell me who piloted the bill in the house and who led the debate on it?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Naturally, it is the member for Laurier who introduced the bill in the house and who led the debate on it, but as the minister himself stated yesterday evening, the member for Laurier had his own responsibilities and could not go beyond the powers he had under the act. As a minister of the crown, does the Minister of Transport have the right to go beyond the powers vested in him by the act? No.
In conclusion, I will say that I would not have been surprised had I been asked that question by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon), because he has not had the same training as the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville. At least, the latter is a lawyer and he should know about the requirements of the law. Apparently, that is not the case.
So, you have two alternatives-he is not aware of the law or he is being unfair; you cannot have it both ways. The law is there, and it outlines the powers of the president of the St. Lawrence seaway authority.
Mr. Chairman, I prefer a learned agronomist to an ignorant lawyer like the hon. member for Laurier.
On a point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

The hon. member for

Why has he not seen to it then that the authorities of the St. Lawrence seaway consider the problem of the Richelieu waterway, while it was time, that everything was organized to make a full study of it, and especially economic studies?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

Mr. Chairman, I shall answer the question of the hon. member who is asking me why I did not have the matter of deepening the Richelieu looked into in my capacity as chairman of the St. Lawrence

seaway authority. This matter is of the utmost importance for the people in the area and it is therefore essential that it be studied as would, I hope, the deepening of the Ottawa river. To establish whether a project will be profitable, one must study it, a technical committee must be instituted. One can-

You could have done it.

Established under a Liberal regime.

Mr. Chairman, after that short period of stormy discussion, I am sure the house will be happy to bear with me during a few minutes in a more serene atmosphere. I do not wish to hold up unduly the debate on this first item. But let me discuss for a few minutes a matter of extreme importance which concerns me very much. That is the municipal airport of the city of Matane.
I realize, Mr. Chairman, the great difficulties and the many problems the Minister of Transport must face because of the exceptional and tremendous progress made in the last few years in the field of air transport and airports facilities.
In my region there are three airports: those of Matane, Mont Joli and Rimouski.
It is not my function to persent here requests concerning the Mont Joli and Rimouski airports, nor does it behoove me to criticize or minimize their requests.
I have here, Mr. Chairman, two good size files which represent quite a considerable amount of work. Since I have become member for Matapedia-Matane there has been a huge correspondance between the Department of Transport and the municipal council of Matane, the chamber of commerce of Matane and other citizens interested in the problem.
I would not want to go too far back and to recall every single step I took for the improvement of the municipal airport in my county seat.
May I be permitted, however, to mention that from the day I was elected in 1958, I have relentlessly attacked that problem. Unfortunately the results I have obtained so far amount to nil.
Shame.

At times, however, we had hopes. I would like to say for the record that on September 15, 1958, I received a letter from an official of the Department of Transport. It went as follows:
The department is preparing the plans lor additional facilities at the Matane airport. The necessary funds have been provided for in the department's supplementary estimates and we are doing everything we can to award the contract as soon as possible.
On March 20, 1959, I received a letter from the then minister of transport. Allow me to read a paragraph of that letter:
As you are aware, an item of $100,000 had been included originally in my department's estimates for the next fiscal year, in the hope that those
Supply-Transport
funds would enable us to finish the plans and at least undertake the works. Unfortunately, we had to cut down our estimates so that the total amount would not exceed that of the current year and, consequently, we had to leave out a certain number of items, including the one concerning the Matane airport. I realize that the city of Matane-
Mr. Chairman, needless to add that the letter was as unpopular with those immediately concerned-and I have no intention of dissociating myself from that group-as with the people of Matane and the surrounding area.
Since that date, I nevertheless energetically pursued my efforts in favour of the improvement and development of the Matane airport. However, on March 13, 1961, the Quebecair company, which served the Matane airport, the north shore and cities like Quebec and Montreal, notified us that it would abandon the service at Matane airport.
I should add that another company remains, with headquarters at Matane, Matane Air Services which is now using our airport for its north shore route. The company operates DC-3 aircraft and also smaller ones-I forget their name-which can carry up to 12 passengers.
If my information is correct, legislation on air security does not, at this time, allow DC-3 aircraft to be used at the Matane municipal airport, and it is because they have a special permit that Matane Air Services may do so.
Now, Mr. Chairman, as I mentioned earlier today, it is useless to go backwards. Up to now, our efforts have been in vain. But we still have the merit of having tried, at least I hope so. Nevertheless, one fact remains: what is done is done and to us all that matters is the present and future.
Quebec Air Lines have abandoned their Matane service and there are now only the Matane Air Services left, with headquarters at the airport. The latter gives adequate service for emergency transportation, that is transportation required by north shore towns. At this time, all concerned have plenty of good will. When I say all concerned, I mean the municipal council of Matane, the chamber of commerce there, the people of Matane and the surrounding area, that is the valley which brings business to the airport of Matane.
At this stage of my remarks, may I say to those who doubt that the traffic at the airport of Matane is considerable, that just a few weeks ago, in a single day, Matane Air

Supply-Transport
Services transported 240 people from Matane to Shelter Bay, to Port Cartier and other small airports along the north shore.
I received this very day a letter from the town council of Matane, to which was attached a copy of a resolution passed by the council. It reads as follows:
Excerpt from the minutes of the proceedings of the municipal council of the city of Matane;
Sitting held on Monday, May 1st, 1961 in the town hall of Matane, at 8 o'clock p.m.;
Members presents: His Honour the Mayor, Mr. F. Adrien Gauthier; aldermen Antoine Lavoie, Rene Pelletier, Benoit McMullen, Raymond Meu-nier, Fernand Dugas, Victor Fournier and J. B. Dionne, secretary-treasurer;
The following resolution was unanimously passed;
Moved by Benoit McMullen, seconded by Fernand Dugas:
Whereas correspondence has been exchanged between the city of Matane and the Department of Transport with regard to the extension and improvement of the municipal airport;
Whereas this request has been turned down by the treasury board as too costly;
Whereas a DC-3 air service is required for adequate operations between the two shores and particularly for the work now under way in the Manicouagan district, where approximately 10,000 men are employed;
Whereas the majority of those employed are from this area and need air service to travel in and out of the area;
Whereas to ensure the efficiency of such a service, particularly at peak periods in the fall and winter, it is essential to use several DC-3s between Matane and the seven stations serviced along the north shore;
Be it unanimously resolved that the city council urges the Hon. Leon Balcer, Minister of Transport, to extend the main runway by 1,000 feet on city owned property, as a substitute for the previous projects which have been found too costly.
In passing such a resolution, I think the Matane city council showed exceptional practical sense, as it gives the authorities a last chance to realize that the city of Matane is entitled to some assistance in the improvement of its airport.
We are asking for a 1,000 foot extension to the runway, and lighting facilities at the airport to permit night landings.
Mr. Chairman, I now close my remarks on behalf of the Matane airport. I feel sure that the present minister, who is very conscious of his responsibility as Minister of Transport, will devote his full attention and consideration to this project which is important both to my constituents and to the hon. member for Matane.
Before resuming my seat, I wish to say a word or two on another timely subject which is of interest to the C.N.R.
The Matapedia valley has a community by the name of Amqui, which is the seat of Matapedia county. The C.N.R. station at
[Mr. Belzile.l
Amqui serves the neighbouring communities of St. Leon le Grand, St. Zenon, Ste. Irenee, St. Tharcisius, St. Vianney. For many years, we have had a 24 hour operator service there. While I was visiting Amqui recently, the station master told me he had received a letter from the C.N.R. dispatcher saying that the night shift would be abolished as of May 22 next.
I believe such an attitude of the C.N.R. would certainly be prejudicial to the passenger traffic of the Matapedia valley and especially to the communities I mentioned a moment ago, because during that shift, three passenger trains stop at Amqui to take or leave passengers. There is the Maritime Express, between Montreal and Halifax; the Ocean Limited between the same points and the Maritime Express on its way back from Halifax to Montreal.
I made the necessary representations to the Minister of Transport and I repeat them here and ask him to use his influence on Canadian National Railway authorities in an effort to have them decide to maintain the operator service at Amqui as it is now and as it has existed for many years.

the second reading of Bill No. C-27, to amend the Senate and House of Commons Act (Solicitor General's eligibility).
He said: Mr. Speaker, in rising to introduce the subject matter contained in this bill may I preface my formal remarks by saying that there is no thought whatsoever, nor do I think there should be, of connecting the principle of the bill with any individual who may hold the office at the moment, may have held it in the past or may hold it in the future. The bill deals in a purely objective way with the position itself. The salary of the solicitor general is the same as that of every cabinet minister except the Prime Minister, namely, $15,000 a year plus $2,000 per annum motor car allowance.
There is also protection in Section 14 in the Senate and House of Commons Act to the extent that the solicitor general and other members of the cabinet shall not be disqualified from sitting in the house by reason of accepting this particular salary from the crown. I think upon examination we shall find that the position of the post of solicitor general is different from that of each of his colleagues in the cabinet. I would say again

Senate and House of Commons Act that when I use any personal pronoun here, it is not meant in a specific sense but only in relation to any individual who might hold the office and the office itself. It is not meant in any personal way. However, the solicitor general is in a different position from that of the other members of the cabinet. I think his post is considered to be somewhat inferior to other cabinet posts.
In this regard I point out the fact that there are a number of references to the post of solicitor general in various statutes of Canada, and that each of them makes a distinction in so far as this post is concerned with respect to the question of motor car allowance. As you will recall, Mr. Speaker, I raised this matter on a previous occasion as a question of privilege which, regardless of the opinions expressed at that time by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton), I think is still valid. However, this is not the time at which to go into that matter. With respect to the motor car allowance of $2,000, in the Appropriation Act No. 5 of 1931, which is chapter 61 of the statutes of that year, vote 352 reads as follows:
To provide for payment annually from the consolidated revenue fund of the sum of $2,000 to each minister of the crown charged with the administration of a department, the Solicitor General, and the Leader of the Opposition,-
Then it goes on to deal with other matters. However, I point out that there is a distinct reference to the solicitor general's office as being somewhat apart and different from that of other ministers. The Salaries Act likewise, which establish as the amount of salary for members of the cabinet, also draws a distinction between the post of solicitor general and each of the other cabinet posts and, in fact, it sets apart the salary of the solicitor general in a separate section from that relating to the other cabinet ministers.
Even when it comes to the method of appointing the person to the office of solicitor general, we find that a distinction is made and that the solicitor general is not appointed, as the other acts say, by virtue of the great seal of Canada. This is notably appointment by the crown. The solicitor general is appointed by his other colleagues in the cabinet or by the governor in council. There again a distinction is drawn.
Even when we came to consider the estimates of the Department of Justice with which the solicitor general is associated, we have found on at least one occasion that it was not necessary or feasible to have the presence of the solicitor general in the committee when the estimates were being considered; and on one occasion when this matter was raised in 1959, the Minister of Justice indicated that he was the officer or the minister
responsible for the Department of Justice and would accordingly deal will all aspects of that particular department.
Last session I made an inquiry of the Prime Minister with respect to the duties, functions and responsibilities of the solicitor general. The answer is contained in Hansard of February 10, 1960, at page 919 and continuing over onto page 920. Perhaps it would be in order for me to quote a part of the answer given by the Prime Minister. He stated in part as follows:
The only order in council under which the solicitor general at present exercises any statutory functions is order in council P.C. 1959-1113 of August 27, 1959, under which he acts as minister of justice in the absence of the Minister of Justice. However, as one of the legal members of the cabinet he advises the Governor General on the exercise of the prerogative of mercy in all cases except capital cases, and in all capital cases he reports to cabinet.
Then the Prime Minister goes on to make mention of the fact that this is a post which does not have heavy departmental responsibilities and that from time to time the solicitor general may have given to him other assignments. For my part I think the post of solicitor general, with its present attachment of responsibilities which I consider to be extremely light, is nothing more than a high or overpaid position of parliamentary secretary. I think the duties, functions and responsibilities of the solicitor general, as they are at the present time, do not warrant that position either being of cabinet rank or commanding a cabinet salary.
The purpose of the bill may be by some considered to be a bit facetious but it seeks to remove the present protection in section 14 of the Senate and House of ommons Act in so far as the eligibility of the solicitor general is concerned to sit in the house as a member. If the bill passes, two alternatives would be open in so far as the post of solicitor general is concerned. One would be that the position of solicitor general could be held by a member of parliament and that no emolument would be attached to it other than the indemnity of a member. The other alternative would be that the post of solicitor general could be held by someone who is not a member of parliament but is an officer within the department.
I might say that a further clause of the bill provides that it is to come into effect on March 31, 1961. At the time of preparation of the bill it was hoped that it might receive the speedy attention of the house and might perhaps be considered before that date. This date, however, can easily be changed. While the reference is to March 31, 1962, in the bill itself, it is not a hard and fast integral part of the bill.


We know that the Department of Justice is a very extensive one and that it embraces a number of extremely important and complex fields. In fact, this situation was recognized by parliament during the last session when parliament authorized the creation of two associate deputy minister posts within the department.
I should like to make a brief reference to some of the extremely important matters which come under the Department of Justice. One is the administration of the Parole Act, which is extremely important in so far as rehabilitative measures are concerned for people who run afoul of the law. There is also the penitentiaries branch, which is another extremely important section of the Department of Justice and deals with the administration of justice and the meting out of penalties. It is also not dissociated from the administration of the Parole Act.
There is also the question of the administration of justice in the Yukon and Northwest Territories, which cover a very large area and where very complex matters arise. There is the subject matter of the Criminal Code and all the various fields with which the code deals.
There is the function of providing legal advice to the crown. There is the all-important operation of the combines investigation branch and the restrictive trade practices commission, their hearings and possible court cases which arise therefrom. Then there is the administration of the Bankruptcy Act, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, salaries of judges, and so on.
I think that if we are to retain the post of solicitor general we should recognize the fact that it is a post worthy of more than the sort of scanty responsibility which is attached to it at the present time. I think we should place the solicitor general in a position comparable with other members of the cabinet by establishing some definite departmental responsibility for the post in order that the rank and salary attached to the position will bear some equitable relationship to its responsibilities.
I should think, for argument's sake-and this is not said in any way to detract from the abilities of the present Minister of Justice -that the operations of the combines investigation branch and restrictive trade practices commission, each connected with the other, could very well be two of the functions of the Department of Justice for which the solicitor general could have some ministerial responsibility.
We could say this about the administration of the Parole Act or the penitentiaries branch,
19, 1961
Senate and House of Commons Act for argument's sake, or any of the other matters over which the Department of Justice has jurisdiction which could also be lumped together and the department in some way or other divided in so far as the responsibility of a cabinet member for those functions is concerned.
If the government would consider dividing the Department of Justice in this way in terms of ministerial responsibility, it would place the office of solicitor general in a much more decent light than I think it is in at the moment. As I have said, at the moment it has some sort of scanty or light responsibilities attached to it which result in it being nothing more than a highly paid position of parliamentary secretary. I think this particular post warrants much greater attention than it receives at the moment.
The initial purpose of the bill is to allow either one of two alternatives; that is, we either have a solicitor general to whom no salary is attached and who at the same time is eligible to sit in the House of Commons as a member, or we have the position of solicitor general as one which is official within the department but which does not allow the person holding that position to sit in the House of Commons as a member.
If the government will consider attaching more responsibility to the post of solicitor general, giving it greater recognition than it has in the past, and if it will cease looking upon this post as a position in which to put somebody who comes from a particular part of the country which should have representation in the cabinet, then I think there would be much greater respect for the post not only in the house, not only in the government but in the whole country.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I am extremely pleased to have this opportunity to introduce Bill No. C-29, an act to amend the Representation Act. The purpose of the bill is very simple, namely to change the name of the electoral district of Humboldt-Melfort to that of Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale.
The present name of the constituency, Humboldt-Melfort, was established under the Redistribution Act of 1952. Prior to that time there were two federal constituencies in existence, namely Humboldt and Melfort. Since that change, within the federal constituency of Humboldt-Melfort, the town of Tisdale and district has been added. The name of Tisdale also appears as one of the provincial constituencies in Saskatchewan. The people of Tisdale and district feel that, although no injustice was done to them through omitting the name of Tisdale, in all fairness it should be added to the names Humboldt-Melfort so that it would then be Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale.
Representations in this regard were first made to me in 1959 when I was home during the parliamentary recess. The Tisdale district chamber of commerce invited me to attend a meeting, having been in touch with me by letter. A letter was directed to Mr. Caston-guay, the electoral officer for Canada, which I should like to read into the record at this point. That letter is as follows:
Re: Humboldt-Melfort constituency
The matter of the name of our constituency was discussed at our recent chamber of commerce meeting.
As you know, this constituency includes the three major towns of Melfort, Humboldt and Tisdale. We feel that the size of Tisdale is such that it should be included in the name of the constituency.
We would be pleased to hear your comments in this regard.
This letter is signed by Mr. W. R. Hod-gins, the secretary of the chamber of commerce, and is dated October 5, 1959.
I have not read the reply to that letter but apparently Mr. Castonguay advised the

chamber of commerce that it was not within his jurisdiction to suggest or effect a change in name, but tnat on occasion private members introduced public bills in the House of Commons which were approved.
I received a telegram from the district chamber of commerce on May 18, 1961 which reads as follows:
Tisdale and district chamber request the name of Tisdale be added to the name of Humboldt-Melfort federal constituency-Tisdale and district chamber of commerce. W. R. Hodgins.
I should like to point out that this bill was introduced by me for the first time in 1960, but did not come before the house for approval before now. During this time no objection has been registered by any town, organization or individuals in the constituency, nor has any political party expressed any objection to the name of Tisdale being added to that of Humboldt-Melfort.
During the last few years the town of Tisdale and district has increased considerably in population and has also assumed a very prominent position as a distributing point for the Carrot river valley. This district is also known as a very productive farm district, evidence of which can readily be seen in the district.
Tisdale is known as the centre of the rape-seed industry in the west. Need I say more, Mr. Speaker? This fact alone has put Tisdale and district on the map as being the pioneer area in this very important grain industry in the west. Had it not been for the Tisdale rapeseed producers, and their early pioneering adventures in this field, Canada would not have been known in the world as the land where some of the best rapeseed is produced.
As a result of this worth-while undertaking by Tisdale inhabitants, the prairie farmers in the west have been able to diversify their grain production, thus taking thousands of acres out of wheat production, and have produced rapeseed, for which there is a tremendous export market available at the present time.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that this is not the time to speak on rapeseed, but it is very important and relevant to the growth and importance of Tisdale.

speechtext:
Room 701, Metcalfe Building, 88 Metcalfe Street,
Ottawa, Ontario.
May 15, 1961.
The Honourable Donald M. Fleming,
Minister of Finance,
Confederation Building,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Sir,
I wish to refer to the annual consultations which have just been concluded between the Canadian government and this embassy about voluntary controls to be applied by Japan on the export of certain products to Canada in respect of the year 1961. As you know, the items we discussed were certain textile products, rubber footwear, plywood, stainless steel table flatware, transistor radios, polyester staple buttons, vinyl raincoats, and receiving tubes for radio and television.
I am now pleased to inform you that as a result of the consultations my government has decided to apply in respect of the calendar year 1961 voluntary export controls as set forth in the annexes to this letter.
Quotas will be allocated to Japanese exporters or producers so that shipments will be spread fairly evenly over the year, the quotas for textile goods, flatware and plywood being allocated on a quarterly basis, with due allowance for the fact that the demand in Canada for some of the quota items is seasonal in nature. However, it should be noted that in respect of a few items there are no actual quota allocations, exports being controlled by a different system.
I wish to take this opportunity to reiterate that, as I mentioned in my letter dated April 29, 1960, these measures are taken by the Japanese government on its own accord in order to conform with its established policy of gradual increase of Japanese exports on an orderly basis with a view to avoiding undue injury to the domestic industry of importing countries. It is the view of the Japanese government that export volumes of the controlled items should normally increase from year to year having regard to market conditions in Canada. Taking into consideration the adverse conditions in the Canadian textile industry and the general economic
situation in Canada, the export quotas for almost all of the textile products have been set for 1961 at the same levels as those for 1960. With the improvement of the situation in the Canadian market my government will naturally anticipate gradual increases in these export quotas in future years.
The quota figure indicated in the annex for stainless steel table flatware represents a large scale reduction of the previous year's export quota and therefore in terms of the concept of orderly growth constitutes an exceptional decision by my government for the year 1961. This decision has been taken in consideration of the difficult business conditions of the Canadian flatware industry as described by Canadian government authorities during the consultations. This exceptional reduction should not be regarded as a precedent in relation to future years or other products.
Furthermore, I should like to remind you again of what I stated in my letter dated April 29, 1960, to the effect that the Japanese government attaches the utmost importance to avoiding a situation where third countries are able to expand their sales to Canada of the products placed under Japanese export control by virtue of the fact that Japan has undertaken to limit her shipments. Should it transpire that such diversion of trade is taking place, I would hope your government would be willing to enter into consultation with my government at any time my government believes that developments warrant it in order to protect Japan's legitimate interests.
In communicating this information to you, I assume that in respect of the products listed in the annexes, for which firm quantities are specified, Canada will not, during the year 1961, invoke the provisions of article XIX of the GATT or those of the exchange of letters annexed to the agreement of commerce of 1954 between Canada and Japan.
I take this opportunity to renew my firm belief that by applying these self-restraining measures we help to pave the way for further expansion of two way trade on an orderly basis, to the mutual benefit of both countries.
Yours sincerely, Toru Hagiwara Ambassador
